domain: Why occupational psychology abandoned the practice of matching employees to jobs via fixed personality-type inventories, and what dislodged a diagnostic tool it once treated as settled science
topic: Why occupational psychology abandoned the practice of matching employees to jobs via fixed personality-type inventories, and what dislodged a diagnostic tool it once treated as settled science

source.title: Why Is Everyone In Tech So Sad?

movement.gist: State plainly: organizational psychology once held, as settled professional consensus, that a worker's underlying personality type could be reliably typed and then matched to the job structure best suited to it — and built an entire selection and coaching industry on this claim.

Reread the claim and start narrowing it by denial: this was not a claim about temperament influencing work style in some loose sense (too weak to have built an industry on), and not a claim merely about self-understanding or team communication (too therapeutic to justify hiring decisions) — the actual claim under scrutiny is the harder, load-bearing one: that type predicts performance well enough to justify selection and placement decisions.

Isolate the single condition the whole edifice depended on: that a person's measured type would be stable across repeated administration and across time, because without that stability there is nothing for a type-based placement to be matching against — a moving target can't be 'matched.' Walk through why this condition seemed uncontroversial for decades: instruments were internally consistent, administrators were trained, correlations with self-report looked orderly, and the entire testing apparatus (norming samples, certification programs, licensing exams for administrators) was built as though stability were an established fact rather than an assumption still owed a direct test.

Test the condition against what actually happened once retest studies were run at scale: a large fraction of respondents were classified into a different type on retake within weeks, with no intervening change in the job or the person, and predictive validity for performance outcomes stayed near baseline across meta-analyses. The condition failed empirically, not marginally. State the verdict: the field was right to abandon type-matching as a selection tool, though it still owes an account of why so much workplace practice — coaching, team-building, self-narrative — keeps the vocabulary alive after the diagnostic claim died.

tension_system.content_frame: Date the shift to the period roughly bracketed by the 1990s Big Five consolidation and the 2000s replicability crisis in personality measurement. Reconstruct the mid-century confidence of type-based selection tools (the sorting logic, the promise of matching temperament to task, the institutional machinery of certified administrators and normed reports) at full strength before showing what broke it: the discovery that type categories don't predict job performance better than chance-adjacent baselines, that test-retest reliability for 'type' was far lower than practitioners assumed, and that the entire selection industry kept using the instruments anyway for reasons unrelated to their validity.

answers.reasoning: Passage argues type-matching rightly retired for failing stability test, vocabulary persists unexplained.

Shows non-boundary placements could still outperform, undermining blanket retirement; rival D also weakens claim somewhat.
Aftermath refers to unexplained survival of vocabulary despite discarded diagnostic evidence base.
